question: What does df.take(n) do?
options: Returns the first n rows as a list of Row objects to the driver
Returns a new DataFrame limited to n rows
Removes the first n rows from the DataFrame
Counts the first n rows
explanation: take(n) is an action that returns the first n rows of the DataFrame as a Python list of Row objects on the driver.

question: How does take(n) differ from limit(n)?
options: take(n) is lazy while limit(n) is an action
They are identical in every way
take(n) is an action returning a list; limit(n) is a transformation returning a DataFrame
take(n) returns all rows; limit(n) returns one
explanation: take(n) immediately returns a list of rows (action), whereas limit(n) is a lazy transformation returning a new DataFrame you can chain further.

question: Why is take(n) more efficient than collect() for previewing data?
options: It compresses the rows before returning
It sorts the data first
It caches the DataFrame automatically
It only retrieves n rows instead of the entire dataset
explanation: take(n) scans just enough partitions to gather n rows, avoiding pulling the whole dataset to the driver like collect() does.

question: What does first() return, in relation to take()?
options: The same as take(1) but returning a single Row instead of a list
The last row of the DataFrame
A DataFrame with one row
The count of rows
explanation: first() returns a single Row (the first one), which is essentially take(1)[0].

question: Without an orderBy(), which rows does take(n) return?
options: Rows sorted by the primary key
Whatever rows Spark encounters first, with no guaranteed ordering
A random sample across all partitions
The n largest rows
explanation: Without an explicit sort, DataFrames have no guaranteed order, so take(n) returns the first n rows Spark happens to read, which may vary.
